newsitem.title: USA: Bill would make Calif. lottery winners repay welfare.
newsitem.headline: Bill would make Calif. lottery winners repay welfare.

text.p: California welfare recipients who win prizes in the state lottery would have to reimburse the state for the assistance under a proposed law, a legislator said Tuesday.

If Republican state Senator Tim Leslie's bill is approved, an aid recipient who wins more than $600 in the state lottery would have to pay back to the state and counties all public assistance received over the previous 10 years. But the amount repaid could not be more than half of the person's lottery winnings.
"For example, if a welfare recipient wins a lottery prize of $1 million and they have received $150,000 in state aid, the state will keep $150,000 of their winnings," Leslie told a news conference.
The recently introduced bill needs the approval of the Democratic-dominated state legislature as well as Republican Gov. Pete Wilson.
Leslie's bill was apparently inspired by occasional reports of welfare recipients winning the lottery.

"I believe that it is wrong for individuals on public assistance to gamble with our tax dollars. Therefore if a welfare recipient plays the lottery and wins, it is appropriate that they return a portion of their winnings to the state of California," Leslie said, adding that New York and New Jersey had passed similar laws.

Leslie said his bill was not aimed at punishing people who received public assistance. But he said it was outrageous that a person who had been supported by tax dollars could become an instant millionaire without having to refund the money to the state.
Leslie said he intended to propose an amendment to his bill which would earmark proceeds for a fund to provide more computers for California schools.
